newsHook: You took Crate from one Knutsford shop to Barbershop of the Year at the British Hairdressing Business Awards for a third time, then rebranded to Crate Collective in April with five sites, a co-working model in Manchester and two Midlands openings planned this year, and our readers want to know how the sums work at that scale.
questions: The Manchester site runs as a co-working space for self-employed barbers rather than a staffed shop. Why that model, and how does the money split compared with a traditional site?
You have gone from one shop to five and are planning two more in the Midlands this year. What does the cash flow look like when you open a new site, and how long before it pays for itself?
You give one-to-one support to barbers in the collective. What does that actually involve day to day, and how do you find people worth backing?
Awards have clearly been part of the Crate story since 2021. What has winning actually done for bookings and recruitment, and what did the entries cost you in time?
How do you price across Knutsford, Macclesfield, Northwich, Manchester and Nottingham? Same menu everywhere or tuned to each town?
What would you say to someone opening their first shop this year who thinks they will have five in a decade?
Where does Crate Collective go from here?

newsHook: You ran 30 MR Barbers shops before the pandemic, deliberately cut that in half, rebuilt around franchising and mentoring, and were a Best Business Leader finalist at the Modern Barber Awards 2025, so our readers will want to hear why smaller turned out stronger.
questions: You went from 30 shops to about half that on purpose. What was wrong with 30, and what did you have to let go of to shrink?
How does the MR Barbers franchise model work for the person taking on a shop: what do they pay, what do they get, and what do you refuse to let them change?
You have talked about a 16-point checklist for new staff built around earning more and living better. What is on it, and which point do people fight you on?
Your shops span Suffolk, Essex, Norfolk and Hertfordshire. How do you set prices across towns with very different rents and customers?
After 35 years, what do you now spend money on that you would have called a waste at 25, and the reverse?
What would you tell someone who has one good shop and is being told to open a second?
Where does MR Barbers go from here?

newsHook: You and your brothers built MaxOliver from one Crowborough shop in 2013 into four sites with an academy and photography studio in Brighton, and were finalists for both Best Business Leader and Best Team at the Modern Barber Awards 2025, which is exactly the kind of family-run growth our readers are trying to copy.
questions: Three brothers, four shops. How are the roles and the ownership actually split, and what is the rule for settling an argument?
You taught Oliver barbering and he taught you hairdressing. How much of your training programme today is still built on that in-house approach rather than buying in courses?
The Brighton site includes an academy and a photography studio. Are those profit centres or marketing, and how do you judge whether they earn their space?
Crowborough, Tunbridge Wells, Lewes and Brighton are very different towns. How do you set prices and staffing at each?
What did it cost to fit out the most recent site, and what would you not spend on again?
What is the one thing you would tell someone opening a shop with a sibling or a mate?
Where does MaxOliver go from here?

newsHook: You opened Onyxx in Fforestfach in 2019, took it into a limited company last year and have just been shortlisted for Barber of the Year at the UK Hair and Beauty Awards 2026, and our readers want the business story behind the sharp cuts.
questions: Onyxx started in 2019 inside a gym before moving to its own unit. What did you learn about rent, footfall and control from operating inside someone else's building?
You went limited in 2025 after years as a sole trader. What prompted that, and what has it changed about how you pay yourself and plan?
How do you price in Fforestfach, and how do you hold your prices when a cheaper shop opens down the road?
You describe the standard at Onyxx as discipline and consistency. How do you hire for that, and what do you do when a barber does not match it?
What does a national award shortlist actually do for a single-site shop in Swansea, and did you spend anything to enter?
What would you tell a young barber in South Wales thinking of opening their own place?
Where does Onyxx go from here?

newsHook: You have run a walk-in traditional barbers in Shifnal since 2003, built it to more than 1,100 Google reviews as the highest-rated shop in Shropshire, sponsored Telford Tigers ice hockey for nearly a decade and were a Community Hero finalist at the Modern Barber Awards 2025, and our readers want to know how a small-town shop stays that busy for 22 years.
questions: You are walk-in only in an industry that has gone almost entirely to apps. Why, and what does that do to your takings on a quiet Tuesday versus a Saturday?
Over 1,100 Google reviews is unusual for a single shop. What do you actually do to get them, and have they moved the needle on new customers?
You have been main sponsor of Telford Tigers since 2016. What does that cost, and how do you know it is paying back?
How have your prices moved since 2003, and how do you handle the conversation when you put them up?
How many barbers do you have, and what has kept them with you rather than renting a chair somewhere else?
What would you tell someone opening a traditional barbers in a market town today?
Where does Egerton's go from here?

newsHook: You have turned a Tonge Moor barbershop into a sensory-friendly service for autistic and neurodivergent clients, go into schools to help children get used to having their hair cut, and were a Community Hero finalist at the Modern Barber Awards 2025, and our readers want to know how that work fits alongside running a shop that has to pay its way.
questions: Sensory-friendly appointments take longer and need a quieter shop. How do you price and schedule them so they do not cost you money?
The school visits and the neurodivergent barber work are unpaid or low-paid. What share of your week do they take, and what have they done for the shop commercially?
What did you change physically in the shop for neurodivergent clients, and what did it cost?
How do you find and train barbers who can do this kind of work, and do you pay them differently?
You have been recognised by the NHS, the Sunday Times and now Modern Barber. Which of those actually brought in customers?
What would you tell a barber who wants to serve clients with additional needs but is worried about the time it takes?
Where does Craig's Barber Shop go from here?

newsHook: You opened BS4 Barber Co in St Anne's in February 2024 after 25 years in hair, and within 18 months had been a Modern Barber Awards finalist two years running, most recently for Community Hero in 2025, which makes you exactly the kind of new independent our readers are trying to become.
questions: You opened in early 2024. What did the shop cost to set up, where did the money come from, and what would you cut from that budget with hindsight?
You spent decades in unisex salons before going pure barbering. What does the salon world know about running a business that barbershops usually ignore?
How did you set your prices in St Anne's, and have you moved them since opening?
You have been shortlisted twice in your first two years. How much of that is the shop's day-to-day work and how much is the entry itself?
What does the community side of the shop involve, and how do you keep it from eating the diary?
What would you tell someone in their forties or fifties thinking of opening their first shop?
Where does BS4 Barber Co go from here?

newsHook: You turned up to work one morning to find the locks changed on the chair you had rented for seven years, opened Hairitage within weeks, paid for your colleague to qualify, and then placed second nationally and won the East Midlands region for Barber of the Year at the UK Hair Awards 2025, which is a story every chair-renter reading us needs to hear.
questions: Losing your chair overnight forced your hand. What did it take, in money and weeks, to get Hairitage open, and what would you have done differently with more notice?
You paid for your colleague to become a fully qualified barber. What did that cost, and how did you structure it so it made sense for the business?
Walk-in only with a small team. How do you keep the diary full and the takings steady?
What did you learn about chair rental from the tenant's side that you now apply as the owner?
The shop runs without a website. Where do your customers actually come from, and what do you spend on marketing?
What would you tell a barber renting a chair right now who is wondering whether to go it alone?
Where does Hairitage go from here?

personRole: Co-owners, Headhunters Barber Shop and Railway Museum
company: Headhunters Barber Shop and Railway Museum
newsHook: You have cut hair on Darling Street since 1981, built the world's only barbershop and railway museum around the chairs, and in September 2025 won the inaugural Love Your High Street award by public vote as Northern Ireland's sole finalist, and our readers want to know how a 44-year-old shop stays this relevant.
questions: Two brothers, 44 years. How is the business split between you, and how has that changed as you have got older?
The museum is a registered charity run by volunteers and free to enter. How does it sit alongside the barbershop in terms of space, cost and footfall?
How have your prices and your customer base changed since 1981, and what have you refused to change?
You won the BIRA award on a public vote of more than 2,000. How did you get that many people to vote for a barbershop?
Have you hired younger barbers, and how do you keep them in Enniskillen?
What would you tell someone opening a barbershop in a small town who wants it to still be there in 40 years?
Where does Headhunters go from here?

personRole: Founder and Barber Director, Brazen Men's Hair
newsHook: You opened Brazen in Leith, added a second shop in Polwarth and a 12-week academy, and in December 2025 Brazen took Scottish Barbers of the Year at the first Scottish Barber Awards, and our readers want to know how you built a two-site business and a training arm that fast.
questions: Leith first, then Polwarth. How far apart were the openings, what did the second one cost, and what did you get wrong the first time that you fixed the second?
The academy takes people from zero to job-ready in 12 weeks. Is it a hiring pipeline for Brazen, a separate revenue stream, or both, and what does a student pay?
How do you price in Edinburgh, and where do you sit against the city centre shops?
You have said your aim is to raise the barbering standard in Scotland. What does that look like in a job spec, and what do you pay to get it?
Scottish Barbers of the Year is a brand-new award. Has it moved bookings, and did it cost anything to enter?
What would you tell a young barber in Scotland who wants to open a shop before they turn 30?
Where does Brazen go from here?

newsHook: You run Blacksmith and Sons in Hackney and were a Best Business Leader finalist at the Modern Barber Awards 2025, and our readers want to know how a shop with that profile actually runs as a business: the prices, the team, the retail and what the name is worth.
questions: A well-known shop in Hackney has a queue of barbers who want to work there. How do you choose, and how do you pay: employed, self-employed or chair rent?
What does the profile of the shop actually do for the takings, and how much of the week goes on the things that build it?
How do you price in Hackney, and how far can a shop with a name push its prices before regulars push back?
What share of your turnover is retail product, and what do you do to sell it without turning the chair into a sales pitch?
What did the last fit-out cost, and what would you not spend on again?
What would you tell a barber with a big Instagram following who thinks that alone will fill a shop?
Where does Blacksmith and Sons go from here?
